items.title: OpenAI argues for using perplexity as a shared metric to track AI model progress and inform safety standards amid emerging capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Perplexity and Intelligence
items.summary:
OpenAI's Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki explains that perplexity, a measure of how well AI models predict data, remains a key indicator of AI progress and emerging capabilities. The company advocates for establishing perplexity as a common metric across developers to enhance transparency and safety in AI development.

Pachocki details how improvements in perplexity have correlated with significant advances from GPT-2 through GPT-4 and beyond, including breakthroughs in reasoning and specialized fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. OpenAI has begun publishing internal perplexity measurements to foster a shared scientific basis for evaluating AI progress and safety standards industry-wide.

The post also highlights the accelerating role of AI in its own development, particularly in algorithmic research on pretraining, which may lead to further rapid advances. OpenAI emphasizes the importance of tracking pretraining progress as a stable and informative measure despite evolving downstream benchmarks and capabilities.

items.summary:
This article explains how to run local AI models like Inkling and Qwen on a Windows PC using Unsloth Desktop, enabling private, home-based AI similar to ChatGPT. It covers hardware needs, focusing on GPU VRAM capacity, and how quantized models allow larger AI models to run on consumer-grade graphics cards.

The guide provides practical advice on choosing AI models based on VRAM size, with examples ranging from 8GB to 32GB GPUs, and discusses trade-offs involved in quantization. It aims to help beginners set up their own local AI systems without complex software installations or subscriptions, emphasizing privacy and cost savings compared to cloud-based AI services.

items.title: Developer launches Worker 755, a browser game where players act as subagents to AI managers using real LLMs like Claude and GPT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent
items.summary:
Worker 755 is a browser-based game in which players serve as subagents to AI managers powered by large language models such as Claude, GPT, and Gemini. The AI manager assigns tasks with a 90-second timer, and players complete or skip them, receiving performance reviews based on their actions. The game simulates a workplace environment where the AI orchestrates tasks and evaluates player responses in real time.

Players can use free shifts on servers with starter credits or bring their own API keys to access various AI models. The game offers options for sandbox or live database environments and supports scripted or AI-driven managers. It runs on Node.js and can be deployed locally or via Docker, with configuration options for API keys and resource limits. The project is open source under the MIT license and includes a detailed design specification and testing framework.

items.title: Comparison of sandboxing tools for AI coding agents including nono, Docker Sandboxes, Microsandbox, and OpenShell highlights trade-offs in security, speed, and usability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Sandboxing AI Coding Agents: Nono vs. Docker Sbx vs. Microsandbox vs. OpenShell
items.summary:
This article evaluates four sandboxing tools—nono, Docker Sandboxes, Microsandbox, and OpenShell—used to isolate AI coding agents and mitigate risks from malicious or unintended actions. It compares their sandboxing methods, credential handling, usability features, and security limitations, noting that none have reached full maturity and all have strengths and weaknesses.

The analysis emphasizes the importance of sandboxing due to widespread AI coding agent use and vulnerabilities like prompt injection, which can manipulate agent behavior. It also discusses real-world incidents illustrating the consequences of inadequate sandboxing and highlights gaps common to all tools, such as limited syscall customization and lack of integrated management interfaces.

The article concludes that while sandboxing reduces risk, it is not foolproof, and proper configuration remains critical to limit potential damage from compromised AI agents or hallucinations.

items.title: METR report finds AI models improve coding but struggle with judgment tasks; research raises concerns about crop yield impact from enhanced rock weathering carbon removal [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
items.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR reveals that while AI capabilities in coding are advancing rapidly, models face significant challenges with tasks requiring judgment, such as designing evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments. This highlights limitations in AI's ability to automate complex research and development functions. Meanwhile, research into enhanced rock weathering—a carbon removal method involving spreading crushed rock on farmland—indicates that adding too much material could reduce crop yields, suggesting the approach's carbon capture potential may be smaller than previously thought. These findings underscore ongoing challenges in both AI development and environmental sustainability efforts.

Initially, many AI-generated patches were superficial or incorrect, but recent contributions increasingly address real user issues effectively.

Despite these hurdles, the maintainer values AI-assisted pull requests as they provide concrete starting points for resolving real-world problems, marking a significant change in open-source collaboration dynamics.

items.title: Researchers say enhanced rock weathering for carbon removal may reduce crop yields, limiting its climate impact to under one billion tons of CO2 annually
items.originalTitle: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
items.summary:
Tech companies including Google and Microsoft have invested heavily in enhanced rock weathering (ERW), spreading crushed alkaline rocks on farms to capture carbon dioxide and improve soil quality. However, new preprint studies led by CarbonPlan researchers suggest that applying too much rock could harm crop yields, which would constrain the method's carbon removal potential to less than one billion tons per year. This raises concerns about the scalability and effectiveness of ERW as a climate solution.

Enhanced rock weathering accelerates natural processes by increasing rock surface area to react with atmospheric CO2, potentially locking carbon in ocean sediments over time. While ERW can improve soil nutrients and acidity, benefiting some farmers, the new findings highlight a trade-off between soil amendment benefits and crop productivity. These results add to ongoing scientific debates about accurately measuring ERW's carbon removal and its practical limits in agriculture.

items.originalTitle: Show HN: Apex verify – an independent model writes the checks your AI skipped
items.summary:
Apex verify is a tool that uses a separate AI model to generate additional tests for code changes made by AI coding agents, aiming to catch errors that pass the original tests but do not meet the task requirements. It runs these new checks alongside existing tests on a copy of the code, providing a verdict of ready, not ready, or unknown with evidence, without modifying the original project.

The tool integrates with various development workflows, including GitHub pull requests and Claude Code sessions, and supports multiple testing frameworks. In evaluations on 200 AI-generated code changes, Apex verify identified about 80% of incorrect changes that passed original tests, though it still misses some errors and occasionally flags correct changes. It is designed to enhance confidence in AI-assisted coding by independently verifying that code changes fulfill their intended tasks.

Rex is free, requires no account, supports full self-hosting, and does not share user data. Invitations to the test program are being sent in waves, with a stable public release planned after the testing phase.

items.originalTitle: Podcast: Simulation Can Tell You What Your Agents are Actually Doing: A Conversation with Zhou Yu
items.summary:
Zhou Yu, a computer science professor and AI expert, explains how dynamic simulations can effectively evaluate conversational AI agents whose actions depend on prior responses and non-deterministic language models. She emphasizes that static benchmarks are insufficient and that simulations incorporating diverse personas, goals, and environmental factors provide more accurate testing.

Simulations can be applied throughout the software lifecycle, aiding product design, continuous integration testing, stress testing before deployment, and monitoring production for model drift or third-party tool failures. They also support compliance verification across regions and enable fine-tuning with synthetic data. Detailed logging during simulations offers audit trails for regulatory compliance and failure analysis.

items.title: 22radar.com publishes public audit of AI agent's autonomous work signing and error tracking, revealing gaps in content verification controls [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Our AI agent signs its own work; we publish its mistakes in a public audit
items.summary:
22radar.com conducted a public audit of its AI assistant, Claude by Anthropic, which autonomously signed its own work but produced errors that were openly documented to enhance transparency. The audit revealed that while controls over the AI's actions and publishing approvals were effective, there were significant shortcomings in verifying the truthfulness of the AI-generated content, including missing validity indicators and independent checks.

The audit detailed a timeline of 39 error instances linked to repeated causes, showing that corrections were made individually without systemic error detection. The site’s crypto rankings were anchored on a blockchain test network with dual signatures from the AI and the owner, but automatic publishing was halted due to GitHub restrictions, requiring manual updates. The findings highlight the challenges in AI governance, particularly in ensuring content accuracy and maintaining a single source of truth across deliverables.

items.title: Sashiko AI adds Linux Performance Specialist review stage to linux_patch_review with benchmarking and false-positive tracking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Sashiko AI Introducing Linux Performance Specialist Review Stage
items.summary:
Sashiko AI has introduced an optional Linux Performance Specialist review stage to its linux_patch_review tool, aiming to improve detection of performance regressions in kernel patches. This stage integrates specialized analysis with benchmarking and false-positive tracking to enhance evaluation accuracy for non-trivial code changes in C, Rust, or struct/header files.

The new review stage includes second-order side-effect tracing, anti-noise guardrails, and a balanced benchmark suite of 40 commits combining upstream regressions and clean commits. Testing showed a significant increase in positive detection rates with minimal false positives and moderate resource overhead, supporting more reliable performance assessments during patch reviews.

items.title: Local AI Tool Engine moves planning into code to improve reliability of small local LLM agents for multi-step tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Make small local LLMs reliable agents by moving planning into code
items.summary:
Local AI Tool Engine (L.A.T.E.) is a new framework that enhances the reliability of small local large language models (LLMs) by shifting the planning logic from the model into plain code. This approach enables the model to focus on generating text while exact computations, file operations, and multi-step workflows are handled by dedicated tools and code, improving accuracy and consistency even with smaller models.

L.A.T.E. supports tasks like web search, file reading and writing, math calculations, and memory across chats, running locally with models from Ollama, LM Studio, or OpenAI-compatible APIs without requiring paid services or complex dependencies. The system executes jobs step-by-step, reports exact outcomes, and avoids hallucinations by relying on real tools for factual operations. It offers both terminal and browser interfaces and automatically manages dependencies and model selection.

items.title: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produces machine-verifiable proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem using novel strategy in Lean, leading Autoform-Hard benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy
items.summary:
OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra independently generated a formal, machine-verifiable proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem using the Lean proof assistant, marking the first known proof of this 2006 theorem in Lean. The model developed its own proof strategy due to missing foundational elements in the Mathlib library, employing a metric called "capacity" to measure growth in mathematical systems.

This achievement occurred on the Autoform-Hard benchmark, a challenging subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench with 56 tasks that previous models failed to solve within budget. Astra completed the proof after nearly 94 minutes and $21.58 in compute costs, surpassing other models by solving 49 tasks, and currently leads the leaderboard ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2.

items.title: Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford invested billions in Anthropic before its record $81.3 billion IPO, citing strong developer adoption and consistent execution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
items.summary:
Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford made significant investments in AI startup Anthropic prior to its November 2026 IPO, which raised $81.3 billion and valued the company at about $1.5 trillion. These investors were convinced by Anthropic's growing developer preference for its Claude model, rising enterprise adoption, and consistent business execution despite high valuations and competition from rivals like OpenAI.

Notable Capital allocated roughly 10% of its U.S. fund to Anthropic's Series E, noting a shift in developer usage favoring Claude over ChatGPT. GIC began investing after seeing early signs of enterprise traction with Claude Code and led later funding rounds, investing over $4.5 billion for about a 1% stake post-IPO. Baillie Gifford committed $1.5 billion across three rounds, impressed by Anthropic's expansion into legal, life sciences, and cybersecurity sectors and its strong financial performance.

These investments reflect confidence in U.S.-based closed-source AI models amid geopolitical complexities and the belief that developers are key early adopters driving AI growth. The paper returns from these bets have been substantial, marking one of the largest venture-scale windfalls in recent years.

items.originalTitle: AI Bubble Deflating? Dell, Workday on Deck
items.summary:
Tech stocks heavily tied to AI, including Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom, dropped 12-16% following a sharp market selloff, with Anthropic's stock plummeting on its second trading day, signaling fears of an AI bubble deflating. Oracle issued a statement denying reports of funding issues for its OpenAI data center deal, reflecting sensitivity around AI financing concerns.

Additionally, SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a $1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix but has since abandoned the idea, which was widely viewed as unrealistic given SoftBank's stretched balance sheet and regulatory hurdles in South Korea. These developments highlight growing skepticism and volatility in AI-related investments.

items.originalSummary:
Friday’s tech stock bloodbath prompted much gnashing of teeth over the weekend. With stocks most exposed to AI—such as Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius—falling in the 12-16% range, and Anthropic tanking on its second day of trading, it felt like the air has finally gone out of the AI bubble. Indeed, worries about AI financing are so intense that Oracle issued a statement late on Friday proclaiming that it had raised all the money it needed for its big OpenAI data center deal and any report that said otherwise was wrong—suggesting it’s a little sensitive about things.

Meanwhile, The Information captured the craziness of the AI bubble with a report late Friday that SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son had explored doing a trillion dollar buyout of SK Hynix. We should emphasize ‘explored’ in past tense—SoftBank said the idea was no longer being pursued. That’s good because the idea is sheer fantasy. SoftBank’s balance sheet is already stretched, thanks to the loans it has taken out to invest in OpenAI. How would Son imagine he could raise the hundreds of billions needed to buy Hynix (leave aside the fact that the South Korean government would be unlikely to ever allow such a deal). What brand of crack is he smoking?

items.title: How Amazon Plays the Long, Expensive Data Center Game That Neoclouds Can’t [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Amazon Plays the Long, Expensive Data Center Game That Neoclouds Can’t
items.summary:
INDIANA, Penn.—A visit this week to an Amazon data center project in Pennsylvania coal country gave me a glimpse of the era we all knew was coming: when tech giants lay claim to some of the hardest-to-secure AI infrastructure while smaller cloud providers, which Nvidia has propped up financially, are trying to hang on.

The 4.4-gigawatt campus in Pennsylvania, once home to a 2-GW coal-fired power plant near the economically depressed borough of Homer City, could become one of the largest AI power parks in the country.

Few companies can marshal the resources as readily as Amazon to transform the site from what it was—a Rust Belt relic that once employed thousands of people but released coal dust and arsenic—into an Appalachian hilltop of gas-fired electrons flowing into 36 buildings powering the AI of Anthropic or others.

items.title: How Apple Got Caught Up in Google Search Ads Slowdown [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Apple Got Caught Up in Google Search Ads Slowdown
items.summary:
Google’s shares have fallen 18% since the company reported a sharp slowdown in search advertising revenue growth stemming in part from the increased popularity of its AI features. Google isn’t the only tech company feeling the pain from that shift.

Growth in Apple’s services revenue, which includes a cut of ad revenue Google makes when people search on Apple’s Safari web browser, slowed to 10% in the latest quarter from 12% in the prior quarter, and will cool further in the current quarter, executives said on Apple’s earnings call earlier this month. Reddit also warned in its latest quarterly report that Google wasn’t sending as much search referral traffic to its online forums because of AI-driven changes to search features.

items.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.originalTitle: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.summary:
Welcome, Weekenders! 

Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one.

On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he’d be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed—or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia’s board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won’t rehire Huang. 

One of the most prominent calls for Huang’s return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. “We’re a country of second chances,” Trump said. “He’s a man ... who made some bad decisions.” (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) 

In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week’s very busy conference circuit. 

That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying “there’s no one who can really replace” Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a “remarkable guy” and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as “one of the most iconic CEOs of all time.” 

On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It’s somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn’t initially wanted to act at all.)

“Ackman’s idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote,” said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist—not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. 

Rather than a board coup, Huang’s clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we’ll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI.

The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman’s ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman’s return. I don’t think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company—its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman’s reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang’s reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company’s workforce.

Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn’t like Huang’s rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I’d totally get why!—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Stories of Art”

After weeks like the ones we’ve just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things—a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase “forward-deployed engineer.”

Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven’t gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I’ve been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through “Stories of Art,” a podcast about, yes, art—from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat’s lower Manhattan loft—that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026’s best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what “The Rest Is History” lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of “Stories of Art”—namely, art—I suggest you watch the podcast’s video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it’s nice to actually see what they’re talking about.) 

Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.—Abram Brown 

Reading: “Fruit Fly” by Josh Silver

In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a “modern-day Virginia Woolf,” as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in “Fruit Fly,” a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory’s relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it’s to insist that it’s time for kids. (“I haven’t had an orgasm in years,” she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by “a shadowy, persisting darkness”—a profound case of writer’s block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings.

Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit—uh oh—and takes to heart another author’s comment about the state of the publishing industry: “go dark, go gay.” She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband’s nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. “Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that,” he thinks, snatching a purse. “Someone should tell them to stop.”) Mallory offers to counsel Leo—pro bono, bless her—and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she’s just a daffy do-gooder. (“This is weird,” Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. “This is very fucking weird, but I guess I’ve done weirder things.”) And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: “It’s so bleak—but also somehow so funny?” Much the same can be said about “Fruit Fly” itself.—A.B.

Welcome, Weekenders! 

Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one.

On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he’d be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed—or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia’s board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won’t rehire Huang. 

One of the most prominent calls for Huang’s return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. “We’re a country of second chances,” Trump said. “He’s a man ... who made some bad decisions.” (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) 

In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week’s very busy conference circuit. 

That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying “there’s no one who can really replace” Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a “remarkable guy” and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as “one of the most iconic CEOs of all time.” 

On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It’s somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn’t initially wanted to act at all.)

“Ackman’s idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote,” said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist—not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. 

Rather than a board coup, Huang’s clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we’ll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI.

The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman’s ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman’s return. I don’t think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company—its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman’s reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang’s reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company’s workforce.

Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn’t like Huang’s rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I’d totally get why!—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

After weeks like the ones we’ve just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things—a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase “forward-deployed engineer.”

Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven’t gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I’ve been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through “Stories of Art,” a podcast about, yes, art—from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat’s lower Manhattan loft—that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026’s best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what “The Rest Is History” lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of “Stories of Art”—namely, art—I suggest you watch the podcast’s video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it’s nice to actually see what they’re talking about.) 

Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.—Abram Brown 

Reading: “Fruit Fly” by Josh Silver

In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a “modern-day Virginia Woolf,” as one reviewer has christened her. (“I haven’t had an orgasm in years,” she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by “a shadowy, persisting darkness”—a profound case of writer’s block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings.

Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit—uh oh—and takes to heart another author’s comment about the state of the publishing industry: “go dark, go gay.” She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband’s nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. “Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that,” he thinks, snatching a purse. “Someone should tell them to stop.”) Mallory offers to counsel Leo—pro bono, bless her—and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she’s just a daffy do-gooder. (“This is weird,” Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. “This is very fucking weird, but I guess I’ve done weirder things.”) And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: “It’s so bleak—but also somehow so funny?” Much the same can be said about “Fruit Fly” itself.—A.B.

A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt’s 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in “The Weight,” a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine’s reserves. It’s part of a plan that’s complex in the same way that “Goldfinger” is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. 

Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. “The Weight” very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. “The Weight” does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film’s editing and cinematography.—A.B.

items.title: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO
items.summary:
On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company’s downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials—and assuage concerns.

Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating.

Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations.

As for the broader market’s jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday’s close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
items.summary:
Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that’s just five years old.

What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we’ve had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies—including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic’s success doesn’t mean the IPO market has opened up. “I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic,” Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information.

items.title: Why Anthropic’s VC Investors Aren’t Letting Go [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Anthropic’s VC Investors Aren’t Letting Go
items.summary:
Earlier this week I reported that at least four venture firms were in line to make at least 10 times their investment in Anthropic, whose shares closed up 17% on the first day of trading Thursday. For many venture capitalists and the endowments and foundations that invest in VC funds, the offering is the first step to turning private shares into cash. 

But some VCs want even more of the company: Sequoia Capital and Iconiq had planned to buy more shares at the IPO, a person familiar with the firms’ thinking said. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Accel intended to do the same, Bloomberg News reported Tuesday. And Altimeter CEO Brad Gerstner told CNBC his firm aimed to invest $5 billion in the IPO. Many of these investors already stand to reap billions from Anthropic’s IPO: Iconiq and Lightspeed hold some of the largest VC stakes, valued at over $27 billion each based on the size of their stakes before the IPO.
